I have 8 mu of flat land here in Quzhou. Every year I grow wheat through the winter and then maize in the summer on the same fields — that is what my family has always done, and it is what most people in our village do. It keeps us with grain to eat and grain to sell, so even if one crop has a bad year, the other usually holds.

For the wheat, I will rotary till the ground in early October before planting. My neighbor tried no-tillage for wheat once and the seedlings came up too thin, so I stick with rotary. I buy improved seed from the shop in town, about 30 jin per mu. I put down compound fertilizer before sowing — about 100 jin per mu — and then topdress with urea at jointing if the wheat looks yellow. I irrigate three times: after planting, at green-up, and at grain filling. The pump costs money, but three times is what my sister-in-law does and her wheat always looks better than the fields that only get twice. I spray herbicide once after sowing and then insecticide and fungicide three more times when I see aphids or mildew. If the weather is normal I expect about 1000 jin per mu.

For maize, there is no time to rest after wheat harvest in early June — I plant straight away with no-tillage into the wheat stubble. Everyone does it this way; the window is only about a week. I use hybrid seed, Denghai 605, about one and a half packages per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 80 jin per mu. I irrigate twice in the summer if the rain is not enough. I spray herbicide once and insecticide three times because the corn borer always comes in July. I usually get about 1100 jin per mu.

I thought about planting some cotton, but my husband's back is not good and our son works in the city, so we do not have enough hands for all that picking. Wheat and maize are better for us because the machines harvest them and the grain buyer comes right to the village. It is not fancy, but it is steady, and I know how to manage it.
